PGuard: A Native, Streaming, and Plug-in Guardrail for Multimodal Large Language Models

Alibaba AAIG
September 2026
Abstract

As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving paradigm for both text-only and multimodal large language models, ensuring safety throughout the generation process has become a critical challenge. Conventional external guardrails address this challenge at the cost of additional inference overhead and a potential gap between their safety judgments and the backbone model’s internal representations. Meanwhile, frontier foundation models possess increasingly sophisticated semantic understanding and rich internal representations, offering an opportunity to build safety capabilities directly into the backbone. Motivated by this, we introduce PGuard, a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail that transforms safety monitoring from an external serving dependency into an integrated capability of the backbone model. PGuard directly leverages the backbone’s intermediate representations for token-level safety detection, without altering its original inference pathway or generation behavior. Specifically, dynamic layer gating selectively aggregates residual-stream representations across layers to extract safety-relevant signals during both prefill and autoregressive decoding. To balance detection accuracy and computational efficiency, PGuard supports multiple representation-modeling architectures, including a lightweight stateless variant and sequence-aware variants built on multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules. Its design also accounts for the execution characteristics of LLM serving frameworks, such as SGLang, optimizing computation and data access to minimize additional runtime and synchronization overhead. As a result, PGuard incurs only 0.820.82–2.26%2.26\% end-to-end overhead on the hundred-billion-parameter backbone Qwen3.5-122B-A10B served by SGLang. Extensive evaluations across more than 30 benchmarks spanning text and multimodal safety, jailbreaks, cyber and CBRN risks, multilingual scenarios, and real-world traffic demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among native guardrails. On text queries with Qwen3.5-9B, PGuard achieves an average F1F_{1} score of 0.836, approaching dedicated external guardrails, while supporting deployment-time configuration of category-specific thresholds and enforcement actions.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive applications, including agentic generation, voice chat, and incremental content rendering. In these settings, model responses are streamed to users as tokens are generated, rather than being presented only after generation is complete, shifting safety moderation from a post-generation task to an online streaming requirement. Specifically, a moderation decision made only after generation completes cannot prevent harmful content that has already been exposed to users. Effective moderation must therefore keep pace with token generation while introducing minimal computational overhead to remain practical at serving scale.

Existing guardrails address this requirement through two broad approaches. External guardrails, such as Qwen3Guard [Zhao and others, 2025], employ separate models to classify user inputs and model responses. Although they can achieve strong detection accuracy, they introduce additional inference costs. More importantly, post-hoc moderation can only identify unsafe content after it has been generated, whereas streaming moderation requires frequent inference by a separate model to detect risks during generation. Furthermore, operating outside the foundation model limits their ability to directly leverage its internal representations. Native guardrails instead exploit signals from the protected model itself. HiddenDetect [Jiang and others, 2025b] detects input-side risks before generation, while NExT-Guard [Fang et al., 2026a] monitors internal features at the token level. Despite this progress, existing native approaches remain constrained by the effectiveness of their safety representations and the runtime cost of extracting and processing them. Our evaluations further show that existing native approaches lag behind leading external guardrails in aggregate detection performance while still incurring appreciable serving overhead.

These limitations motivate a more effective way to leverage the backbone’s internal representations for native safety modeling. The intermediate representations of a frontier foundation model encode rich semantic and contextual information about the content being generated, providing a natural basis for identifying safety risks without duplicating much of the computation performed by a separate guardrail model. However, effectively translating these representations into safety signals raises two challenges. First, safety-relevant features are not uniformly distributed across layers or token positions, making adaptive layer selection important for effective representation extraction. Second, risks may emerge from relationships among tokens and evolve as a response unfolds, which cannot always be captured by classifying each position independently. Addressing these challenges requires both adaptive representation extraction and effective modeling of dependencies across token positions.

To address these challenges, we present PGuard, a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail built on a frozen foundation model backbone. PGuard introduces dynamic layer gating to adaptively select and aggregate residual-stream representations at each token position, enabling the guardrail to capture safety-relevant features across different layers. Based on these representations, PGuard supports two complementary modeling paradigms. The stateless variant classifies each token position independently, while the sequence variants explicitly model dependencies across positions to capture how risks emerge and evolve during generation. We instantiate sequence modeling with multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules, offering different trade-offs between detection quality and computational cost. To enable localized safety supervision without requiring exhaustive token-level annotations, PGuard adopts segment-level supervision, computing loss only at annotated positions and for tasks with available labels. Our experiments show that sequence modeling improves response-level detection over the stateless variant across both text and multimodal tasks.

Beyond detection efficacy, deploying native guardrails efficiently requires coordinating safety computation with the backbone’s generation process. Mainstream language model inference and serving engines (e.g., vLLM [Kwon et al., 2023] and SGLang [Zheng et al., 2024]) coordinate batching, parallel execution, and GPU synchronization to sustain high throughput. Accessing intermediate representations and reporting risk scores introduces additional dependencies into this execution process. In particular, poorly placed synchronization can stall active batches, making the resulting overhead substantially greater than the guard computation itself. PGuard therefore incorporates serving-engine constraints into its execution design. We integrate PGuard with SGLang, aligning risk computation and reporting with the engine’s scheduling mechanisms. The integration supports both stateless and sequence variants without modifying the SGLang codebase. Beyond SGLang, we are currently working on a vLLM integration to extend the same serving-aware execution design to another widely used inference and serving engine.

We evaluate PGuard on more than 30 benchmarks covering text and multimodal safety, jailbreaks, cyber and CBRN risks, multilingual scenarios, and real-world traffic. On text-query benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B, PGuard achieves an average F1F_{1} score of 0.836, approaching that of Qwen3Guard. On multimodal query benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B, it achieves an average F1F_{1} score of 0.741, compared with 0.638 for HiddenDetect and 0.474 for Llama Guard 4. On the 100B-scale Qwen3.5-122B-A10B backbone, end-to-end latency overhead remains below 1.3%1.3\% for stateless and 2.4%2.4\% for sequence variants. These results demonstrate that native guardrails can achieve competitive detection quality while imposing limited overhead on large-scale model serving.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We propose PGuard, a native streaming guardrail that leverages dynamic layer gating to extract token-wise safety representations from a frozen backbone. We further introduce complementary stateless and sequence-based modeling architectures to support both independent token classification and sequential risk modeling.

  • •

    We develop a serving-aware execution strategy that coordinates safety computation with the scheduling and execution mechanisms of model inference engines. Our SGLang integration supports both modeling variants while minimizing redundant computation and synchronization overhead, without modifying the inference engine’s codebase.

  • •

    We conduct extensive evaluations across more than 30 text and multimodal safety benchmarks and real-world traffic. Our analysis demonstrates the benefits of sequence modeling, characterizes the trade-offs between detection quality and serving overhead, and examines the complementary roles of native screening and external adjudication.

2 Methodology

2.1 Problem Formulation and Design Goals

We consider a frozen backbone model, either an LLM or an MLLM, serving multi-turn conversations with text-only or multimodal inputs. A native guardrail leverages the backbone’s intermediate representations to detect risks in user inputs during prefill and in generated responses during decode. Formally, let the backbone process a token sequence x1:Tx_{1:T} and produce hidden states 𝑯(l)∈ℝT×d{\bm{H}}^{(l)}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{T\times d} at layer ll, where the tt-th row 𝒉t(l)∈ℝd{\bm{h}}^{(l)}_{t}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} represents the hidden state at sequence position tt. The guardrail is defined as

g:(𝑯(l1),…,𝑯(lm))↦(𝒓1,…,𝒓T),𝒓t∈[0,1]|𝒴|,g:\bigl({\bm{H}}^{(l_{1})},\ldots,{\bm{H}}^{(l_{m})}\bigr)\mapsto\bigl({\bm{r}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{r}}_{T}\bigr),\qquad{\bm{r}}_{t}\in[0,1]^{|\mathcal{Y}|},

which maps intermediate representations from selected backbone layers l1,…,lm{l_{1},\ldots,l_{m}} to per-position risk scores. Here, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} denotes the shared set of risk categories across safety tasks, and 𝒓t{\bm{r}}_{t} contains the predicted probability of each category at position tt. A position is flagged if the predicted probability of any risk category exceeds its corresponding threshold.

A production-ready native guardrail must satisfy four design goals, which guide the design of PGuard:

  • •

    Competitive detection performance. The guardrail should perform competitively with dedicated external detectors.

  • •

    Native integration with generation. Risk scoring should leverage the backbone’s forward pass, enabling per-position detection during prefill and decode without modifying the backbone’s computation.

  • •

    Low serving overhead. The additional computation should contribute only a small fraction of the end-to-end serving cost, targeting a few percent overhead on production backbones.

  • •

    Broad risk coverage. A unified training framework should support text and multimodal inputs, jailbreaks, multilingual content, and emerging risks under a shared label taxonomy.

Figure 1 illustrates the PGuard architecture. The frozen backbone supplies residual-stream features from selected layers. Dynamic layer gating fuses the captured features at each position, and the fused feature is modeled either by a stateless variant or by a sequence variant based on multi-scale causal EMA-attention or a GRU-based recurrent module. The risk classifiers then produce risk scores under the unified taxonomy during both prefill and decode.

2.2 Multi-Layer Hidden State Extraction

Safety-relevant information is not distributed uniformly across layers. At each capture layer, PGuard reads the residual stream, i.e., the tensor that enters that layer. The capture is read-only and adds no state to the frozen backbone. Training and serving capture the residual stream at matching layer boundaries, reconstructing it from separate hidden-state and residual buffers where necessary (Section 3.1).

Let ℒ={l1,…,lm}\mathcal{L}=\{l_{1},\ldots,l_{m}\} denote the set of capture layers. For a sequence of TT positions, feature extraction produces a tensor 𝑭∈ℝm×T×d{\bm{F}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m\times T\times d}, where dd is the backbone hidden size. In an MLLM, the visual tokens simply occupy positions in the same sequence as text tokens. Thus, image and text evidence is fused by the backbone before feature extraction.

2.3 Dynamic Layer Gating

The most discriminative safety signals can emerge at different depths across inputs and even across positions within the same input. To accommodate this variation, PGuard employs dynamic layer gating in two stages. During calibration-set pretraining, with the backbone frozen, the gate operates over a larger candidate set of layers, and the learned gating profiles determine the capture-layer set ℒ\mathcal{L}. During full training and deployment, the gate operates over this fixed set and adaptively weights the captured representations at each position. We formulate the gate over ℒ\mathcal{L}, with the same formulation applied to the candidate set during pretraining. The gate computes a score for each position-layer pair:

st,i=𝒘g⊤​𝒉t(li),gt,i=𝟙[i∈ℐt]exp(st,i)∑j∈ℐtexp⁡(st,j),s_{t,i}={\bm{w}}_{g}^{\top}{\bm{h}}^{(l_{i})}_{t},\qquad g_{t,i}=\frac{\mathbb{1}[i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}]\exp(s_{t,i})}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\exp(s_{t,j})}, (1)

where 𝒘g{\bm{w}}_{g} is a learned projection and ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} contains the indices of the top-LL layers by score ranked by their scores at position tt. During training, Gumbel noise is added to the scores before selection. In full training and deployment, we set L=|ℒ|L=|\mathcal{L}|, allowing all captured layers to participate while retaining position-specific weights. The fused representation is then computed as

𝒙t=∑i=1mgt,i​𝒉t(li),{\bm{x}}_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_{t,i}\,{\bm{h}}^{(l_{i})}_{t}, (2)

yielding a position-adaptive soft mixture of the captured layer representation. This gating mechanism allows a single training recipe to accommodate backbones of different depths by learning layer preferences independently at each position (Section 4.5 analyzes the learned gating profiles).

2.4 Representation Modeling

The backbone provides contextualized representations at each position, which PGuard can use either directly or through an additional module that aggregates historical evidence. These alternatives offer different trade-offs between detection accuracy and computational cost. Each variant produces a representation 𝒛t{\bm{z}}_{t} for the risk classifiers. Let 𝒙~t=𝑾p​𝒙t∈ℝdp\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}={\bm{W}}_{p}{\bm{x}}_{t}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d_{p}} denote the fused feature projected into a compact space, where 𝑾p∈ℝdp×d{\bm{W}}_{p}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d_{p}\times d}.

Stateless (last-token) variant.

The stateless variant independently classifies each position using its projected feature:

𝒛tsl=𝒙~t,{\bm{z}}_{t}^{\mathrm{sl}}=\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}, (3)

Thus, all operations from the gate output to the logits are position-wise, with no recurrent or cached state maintained during training or inference. This point-wise computation makes the stateless variant the most computationally efficient option: prompt positions can be scored in parallel, while each decoding step incurs only a small additional classification cost.

Sequence variants: EMA-attention and GRU.

The sequence variants maintain a per-request state that accumulates safety evidence throughout generation. We instantiate this paradigm with two designs that offer complementary trade-offs. The EMA-attention design maintains causal exponential moving averages at multiple decay rates for each captured layer, indexed by i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:

𝒎t,i(k)=αk𝒉t(li)+(1−αk)𝒎t−1,i(k),αk=1−e−1/λk,k=1,…,K,{\bm{m}}_{t,i}^{(k)}=\alpha_{k}\,{\bm{h}}_{t}^{(l_{i})}+(1-\alpha_{k})\,{\bm{m}}_{t-1,i}^{(k)},\qquad\alpha_{k}=1-e^{-1/\lambda_{k}},\quad k=1,\ldots,K, (4)

where the fixed decay αk\alpha_{k} is determined by the effective length λk\lambda_{k} of each scale. Shorter scales emphasize recent features, whereas longer scales retain a more slowly decaying summary of the earlier context. The summaries are maintained separately for each captured layer and then fused using the current gate weights, 𝒎¯t(k)=∑igt,i​𝒎t,i(k)\overline{{\bm{m}}}_{t}^{(k)}=\sum_{i}g_{t,i}{\bm{m}}_{t,i}^{(k)}. We construct 𝑺t=[𝒎¯t(1),…,𝒎¯t(K),𝒙t]{\bm{S}}_{t}=[\overline{{\bm{m}}}_{t}^{(1)},\ldots,\overline{{\bm{m}}}_{t}^{(K)},{\bm{x}}_{t}] by concatenating the fused summaries with the current feature. Attention then uses the current feature as the query and 𝑺t{\bm{S}}_{t} as both keys and values:

𝒛tema=𝑾p​Attn​(Q=𝒙t,K=𝑺t,V=𝑺t),{\bm{z}}_{t}^{\mathrm{ema}}={\bm{W}}_{p}\,\mathrm{Attn}\bigl(Q={\bm{x}}_{t},\ K={\bm{S}}_{t},\ V={\bm{S}}_{t}\bigr), (5)

allowing each position to be represented using both its current features and a multi-scale summary of preceding context.

The GRU design instead carries historical information in a gated recurrent unit with state 𝒄t∈ℝdc{\bm{c}}_{t}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d_{c}}, where dcd_{c} is the state dimension. Since all query positions are available during prefill, their projected features 𝒙~t\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} are aggregated in parallel through attention pooling with a learned query vector. The resulting query summary initializes the recurrent state 𝒄0{\bm{c}}_{0}, and the classification path applied to 𝒄0{\bm{c}}_{0} produces the query-side prediction. Starting from 𝒄0{\bm{c}}_{0}, the recurrent state is updated at each response token as follows:

where 𝒗t∈(0,1)dc{\bm{v}}_{t}\in(0,1)^{d_{c}} is the reset gate, 𝒄^t∈ℝdc\hat{{\bm{c}}}_{t}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d_{c}} is the candidate state, and the update gate 𝒖t∈(0,1)dc{\bm{u}}_{t}\in(0,1)^{d_{c}} weights the candidate while 1−𝒖t1-{\bm{u}}_{t} weights the previous state. The skip term 𝑾s​𝒙~t{\bm{W}}_{s}\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} preserves the current position’s own evidence in the output.

2.5 Multi-Task Training

We adopt a shared risk taxonomy adapted from YuFeng-XGuard [Lin et al., 2026], comprising 9 risk dimensions with 29 fine-grained categories spanning general content safety, jailbreaks, multilingual risks, and cyber & CBRN domains. All training sources are mapped into this shared taxonomy (Appendix A), enabling a unified training process across different deployment scenarios. Each task group is equipped with a multi-class classifier over its corresponding categories. The backbone remains frozen throughout training, and only the PGuard module is optimized.

Sample-level labels provide insufficient localization of where risks emerge within a response. Although token-level annotation could provide finer-grained supervision, it is expensive, while safety judgments often require interpreting spans of text in context. We therefore adopt segment-level supervision, retaining each sample as a complete token sequence with multiple annotated segments. Each segment is annotated with labels for the relevant safety tasks, which supervise selected positions near its end. The classification loss is averaged over supervised positions within each segment and across available task annotations. For the GRU variant, the query-side prediction is additionally supervised using the label of the last query segment.

2.6 Streaming Detection and Decision

Per-token risk and verdicts.

For each position and task cc, the classifier outputs a probability distribution Pc(⋅∣x1:t)P_{c}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t}) over the task-specific categories 𝒴c⊆𝒴\mathcal{Y}_{c}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}. A position is flagged for an unsafe category y∈𝒴cy\in\mathcal{Y}_{c} when Pc(y∣x1:t)≥τc,yP_{c}(y\mid x_{1:t})\geq\tau_{c,y}. Each trained PGuard model uses its own calibrated thresholds, configured separately for query and response stages and for text-only and image-text inputs (Appendix B). During prefill, the query-side verdict is derived from scores at selected positions or their aggregation, depending on the application’s policy, and is available before response generation begins. During decode, the hidden state at position tt is used to assess the content up to and including token xtx_{t}, while the same forward pass predicts the next token xt+1x_{t+1}. Verdict consumption is configurable at deployment: applications can selectively enable task groups and determine how flagged content is handled, including reporting, interrupting, or steering generation.

Sampled scoring.

To further reduce serving overhead, PGuard supports sampled scoring, exploiting the observation that safety risks typically manifest across phrases or passages rather than in isolated tokens. Under this option, PGuard performs classification and reports risk scores only once every pp tokens, skipping the classification path at intermediate steps (Section 3.2). For sequence variants, however, the recurrent or attention-based state is still updated at every token, ensuring that each reported score incorporates evidence from the entire processed prefix. The early-interception analysis in Section 4.4 uses the full per-token scoring trajectory rather than sampled scores.

Two-tier deployment.

PGuard also supports a two-tier cascade in which the native variant performs token-level scoring on all traffic, while only flagged content is escalated to an external reasoning guardrail for fine-grained adjudication (Section 4.8).

3 System Implementation

3.1 Inference Engine Integration

We integrate PGuard into SGLang [Zheng et al., 2024], with runtime support for feature capture, per-request state management, and streaming risk-score delivery. The integration supports the stateless, EMA-attention, and GRU variants through a shared engine interface. Figure 2 illustrates the integration.

At each selected layer, the runtime captures the same residual-stream representation used during training (Section 2.2). For backbones that maintain hidden-state and residual tensors separately, the runtime reconstructs this representation by summing the two tensors. This operation is performed solely for feature extraction and does not alter the backbone’s forward computation. The resulting risk scores are exposed as response metadata, leaving the original token logits and sampling path unchanged.

For sequence-based variants, the runtime maintains persistent state tensors for each active request in GPU memory. Each request is assigned a dedicated slot throughout its lifetime, enabling state retrieval independently of changes in batch composition introduced by the scheduler. During both chunked prefill and auto-regressive decoding, the runtime retrieves the state associated with the request, updates it with newly processed features, and writes the updated state back to the corresponding slot. For the GRU variant, prefill does not process query tokens recurrently. Instead, it projects all query features in parallel and aggregates them into the initial state 𝒄0{\bm{c}}_{0} using learned-query attention pooling. The runtime stores 𝒄0{\bm{c}}_{0} as the per-request state. During decode, each response token updates this state incrementally.

Runtime Support for PGuard Variants.

All variants share the same engine interface but differ in state management. The stateless variant requires no persistent state. The EMA-attention variant maintains a set of multi-scale states for each request and captured layer. During chunked prefill, each chunk consumes the final state from the preceding chunk and produces an updated state for the next chunk. During decode, these states are updated incrementally at each token.

The GRU variant maintains a single fixed-size state per request. During prefill, learned-query attention pooling computes the initial state from the query features (Section 2.4), which is then stored in the request’s assigned slot. During decode, each response token updates this state before optional scoring. Consequently, tokens for which no risk score is reported are still incorporated into the recurrent state, preserving the complete response history.

PGuard also supports pipeline and tensor parallelism. Under pipeline parallelism, the Qwen3.5 integration forwards captured features in a fixed layer order and executes the guard at the final stage. Under tensor parallelism, each rank independently computes scores for a distinct subset of sampled prefill positions. The ranks then aggregate their local maximum scores using an all-reduce operation.

3.2 Algorithm–System Co-Optimization

Directly integrating a native guardrail into the backbone forward pass can increase serving latency, even when the guard head is lightweight. The overhead arises not only from risk-score computation but also from repeated kernel launches, sequential state updates, and host–device synchronization.

Stage-level profiling reveals two primary sources of overhead. The first is redundant work. Under PGuard’s sampled reporting policy, risk scores are consumed only at selected positions, yet naively executing the guard at every token incurs unnecessary computation. The second is inefficient execution. Sequential state updates constrain prefill parallelism, small operators trigger repeated kernel launches, and host–device synchronization can stall the submission of subsequent backbone operations.

We address these bottlenecks through coordinated algorithmic and runtime optimizations. Specifically, we decouple state updates from risk scoring by computing risk scores only at positions selected for reporting, parallelize guard-state computation during prefill, move synchronization off the serving critical path, and fuse compatible operations to reduce kernel-launch overhead.

Selective Guard Scoring.

Under a sampled reporting policy, applications consume a risk score every pp tokens. Computing scores at intermediate positions therefore incurs unnecessary overhead. We eliminate this redundant computation by decoupling state updates from risk scoring. For the EMA-attention and GRU variants, every token continues to update the corresponding state to preserve the sequence context, whereas the scoring path is executed only at positions selected for reporting.

SGLang captures backbone and guard operations into a single CUDA graph. As a result, each graph replay executes the entire scoring path, even at positions where the resulting scores are not reported. To avoid this, we split the decode graph into two segments. The first segment covers the backbone forward pass and the sequence-state update, and is replayed at every step. The second segment covers the guard scoring path, and is replayed only at the sampled steps (Figure 3). With a reporting interval of pp tokens, this removes approximately 1−1/p1-1/p of the scoring executions.

Parallel Prefill Execution.

Prefill is the primary source of PGuard’s overhead in our workloads. While the backbone processes prompt tokens in parallel, a straightforward EMA implementation updates the guard state sequentially, one token at a time. These sequential updates limit parallelism and incur repeated kernel-launch overhead. We exploit the linear structure of the EMA update to compute states within each chunk in parallel. For a fixed decay rate αk\alpha_{k}, the state at position tt can be expressed in terms of the state at an earlier position ss as follows.

𝒎t,i(k)=(1−αk)t−s​𝒎s,i(k)+∑j=s+1tαk​(1−αk)t−j​𝒉j(li).{\bm{m}}_{t,i}^{(k)}=(1-\alpha_{k})^{t-s}\,{\bm{m}}_{s,i}^{(k)}+\sum_{j=s+1}^{t}\alpha_{k}(1-\alpha_{k})^{t-j}\,{\bm{h}}_{j}^{(l_{i})}. (7)

We partition the prompt into fixed-size chunks and represent the weighted sums using a lower-triangular decay matrix as shown in Figure 4(a). Multiplying its selected rows by the token features computes the corresponding EMA summaries in parallel. Importantly, every prompt token contributes to these summaries, including tokens at positions where no risk score is reported. We compute the states at sampled positions and the final prompt token for scoring, and retain each chunk’s final state to initialize the next chunk.

Tensor parallelism provides an additional opportunity to distribute prefill scoring as illustrated in Figure 4(b). When each rank independently evaluates the guard on replicated features, the same scores are redundantly computed across ranks. Instead, we evenly partition the sampled positions across the NN ranks, with each rank computing a local maximum score for every risk category over its assigned positions. A single element-wise maximum all-reduce then aggregates these local results into the per-request score vector. Only the score vectors are exchanged, avoiding the transfer of hidden states across ranks. This partitioning reduces the scoring workload on each rank by approximately a factor of NN.

Non-Blocking Guard Execution.

Feature aggregation, context modeling, and score delivery introduce additional data dependencies when a native guardrail is integrated into the serving runtime. Resolving these dependencies through host–device synchronization can delay the submission of subsequent backbone operations. We keep state management and score aggregation on the GPU and use asynchronous transfers to reduce synchronization on the serving critical path. During prefill, fixed-interval sampling decisions are staged in pinned host memory and transferred asynchronously, with the sampled-token mask constructed on the GPU. Per-request state lookup and reset also remain on the GPU. Together, these changes avoid unnecessary host–device synchronization during prefill.

During decode, we overlap risk-score delivery with ongoing engine execution and align result consumption with the engine’s existing synchronization schedule. Asynchronous staging in pinned host memory supports this overlap without introducing an additional synchronization barrier for score delivery.

Fused Guard Computation.

The guard head consists of many small matrix operations, each requiring a separate GPU kernel launch and memory access. For small inputs, these overheads can dominate the actual computation and result in poor GPU utilization. To address this, we fuse compatible operations into larger matrix multiplications. In the multi-task classifier, all nine task heads share the same input features. We concatenate the weights of their first layers into a single matrix and arrange the weights of their output layers into a block-diagonal matrix. This enables all nine heads to be evaluated using only two matrix multiplications, rather than eighteen. The fused weights are constructed once during model loading, eliminating the need for weight assembly during serving. This design reduces kernel-launch overhead and improves GPU utilization.

Together, these optimizations align guard execution with application reporting requirements while preserving complete sequence-state updates. By exploiting parallelism, reducing synchronization, and consolidating small operations, they mitigate the computational and runtime overhead of native guardrail integration along the serving critical path.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

4.1.1 Benchmarks

We evaluate PGuard across four dimensions, following the evaluation settings of WildGuard Han et al. [2024] and Qwen3Guard Zhao and others [2025].

  • •

    Safety classification. ToxicChat Lin et al. [2023], XSTest Röttger et al. [2024], OpenAI Moderation OpenAI [2023], Aegis 2.0 Ghosh and others [2025], WildGuardMix Han et al. [2024], S-Eval Yuan et al. [2024], BeaverTails Ji et al. [2023], Qwen3Guard test set Zhao and others [2025], FineHarm Li et al. [2025b], and SafeRLHF Dai et al. [2024] (text). SPA-VL Zhang and others [2025b], UnsafeBench Qu et al. [2024], MM-SafetyBench Liu and others [2023], VLGuard Zong and others [2024], HoliSafe Lee and others [2025], VLSBench Hu and others [2025], FigStep Gong et al. [2025], and Beavertails-V Ji et al. [2026] (image-text).

  • •

    Frontier risk classification. StrongREJECT Souly et al. [2024], S-Eval jailbreak subset Yuan et al. [2024] (text), FigStep Gong et al. [2025] and MM-SafetyBench Liu and others [2023] (image-text) for jailbreak detection; WMDP Li and others [2024], Meta CyberSecEval 3 Wan and others [2024], and SOSBench Jiang and others [2025a] for cybersecurity and CBRN risk identification.

  • •

    Multilingual safety. PolyGuardPrompts Kumar and others [2025] (17 languages), RTP-LX de Wynter and others [2025] (12 languages), and Lingua-SafetyBench Shi and others [2026] (10 languages).

  • •

    Over-refusal and real-world data. XSTest Röttger et al. [2024] and OR-Bench Cui and others [2025] assess over-refusal. Benign-traffic evaluation uses Alpaca Taori et al. [2023] and WildChat Zhao and others [2024] for text, and ShareGPT4V Chen and others [2023], LLaVA-Instruct Liu et al. [2023], and MMStar Chen and others [2024] for image-text inputs.

4.1.2 Baselines

We compare PGuard with native and external guardrails. Native guardrails derive safety signals from the protected backbone; external guardrails run a separate safety model over the query and response.

  • •

    Native guardrails: GradSafe Xie and others [2024] (Llama-2-7B Touvron et al. [2023]), SIREN Jiao et al. [2026] (Llama-3.1-8B Grattafiori et al. [2024]), NExT-Guard Fang et al. [2026a] (Qwen3-8B), HiddenDetect Jiang and others [2025b] (LLaVA-1.6-7B Li et al. [2024]).

  • •

    External guardrails: SCM-7B Li et al. [2025b] (Qwen2.5-7B Yang et al. [2024]), Qwen3Guard-Stream-8B Zhao and others [2025] (Qwen3-8B Yang and others [2025]), Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B Zhao and others [2025], WildGuard-7B Han et al. [2024], PolyGuard-Qwen-7B Kumar and others [2025], YuFeng-XGuard-8B Lin et al. [2026], LlamaGuard 4 (12B) Meta [2025], LlavaGuard-7B Helff and others [2025].

4.1.3 Implementation Details

Sections 4.2–4.3 evaluate PGuard on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B Qwen Team [2026]. Section 4.6 extends the evaluation to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (also referred to as Qwen3.5-Flash) and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B. We evaluate query and response classification against sample-level benchmark labels. For these classification evaluations, we use a scoring interval of p=10p=10 tokens. Query classification uses the score at the query boundary, and response classification uses the score from sampled token scores. Decision thresholds are calibrated on a held-out validation set.

We evaluate Qwen3Guard-Gen and Qwen3Guard-Stream in strict mode, treating the Controversial label as unsafe. Other baselines use their officially released weights and default settings where available. HiddenDetect and NExT-Guard additionally require calibration because official settings are unavailable.

4.2 Main Results

Text Safety Evaluation

Tables 1 and 2 show that PGuard achieves the highest average text-safety F1F_{1} among the evaluated native guardrails. For queries, PGuard-ema (Qwen3.5-9B) and PGuard-gru (Qwen3.5-9B) both achieve 0.836, exceeding prior native baselines by 4.5–9.5 percentage points. This score is comparable to Qwen3Guard-Stream (0.834) and higher than Qwen3Guard-Gen (0.814). PGuard-ema (Qwen3-8B) achieves 0.827, falling 0.7 percentage points below Qwen3Guard-Stream but outperforming Qwen3Guard-Gen by 1.3 percentage points, both built on Qwen3-8B. For responses, PGuard-gru (Qwen3.5-9B) leads the PGuard variants at 0.860, below Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B (0.866) and YuFeng-XGuard-8B (0.881). On Qwen3-8B, PGuard-ema achieves 0.858, exceeding SCM-7B by 7.6 percentage points and exceeding Qwen3Guard-Stream-8B (0.830).

Sequence variants consistently outperform the stateless variant in average F1F_{1} on both query and response safety across both backbones, with gains ranging from 0.3 to 6.5 percentage points.

Multimodal Safety Evaluation

The same training recipe applies to multimodal backbones, which fuse visual and textual information before PGuard extracts their representations. In Table 3, PGuard-ema (Qwen3.5-9B) achieves the highest average query F1F_{1} of 0.741, compared with 0.638 for HiddenDetect and 0.474 for Llama Guard 4. HiddenDetect remains stronger on MM-SafetyBench and FigStep. For responses, PGuard-gru leads the evaluated methods with an average F1F_{1} of 0.798.

Adversarial Jailbreak Detection.

Table 4 evaluates detection on the static jailbreak benchmarks. PGuard-ema (Qwen3-8B) achieves an average F1F_{1} of 0.946, ranking first among native guardrails and second overall. It trails YuFeng-XGuard-8B (0.972) and exceeds Qwen3Guard-Gen (0.928). On S-Eval-JB, its F1F_{1} of 0.896 exceeds NExT-Guard on the same backbone by 12.5 percentage points, while YuFeng-XGuard-8B leads at 0.944. These results support the effectiveness of internal representations for detecting the evaluated jailbreak prompts.

Cyber & CBRN Risk Identification.

In Table 5, PGuard-lasttok (Qwen3.5-9B) achieves the highest average F1F_{1} of 0.833, followed by the GRU (0.789) and EMA-attention (0.773) variants on that backbone. On Qwen3-8B, PGuard-ema reaches 0.747, exceeding the evaluated native baselines and both Qwen3Guard variants. Performance varies across risk categories: SIREN leads on WMDP biology and chemistry, whereas PGuard leads on several CyberSecEval3 and SOSBench subsets.

Multilingual Safety Evaluation.

Table 6 shows competitive detection across the evaluated languages, with the strongest method varying by benchmark and stage. On PolyGuardPrompts, PolyGuard-Qwen-7B leads query classification at 0.869, and YuFeng-XGuard-8B leads response classification at 0.793. Among native guardrails, PGuard-ema leads both stages, reaching 0.835 for queries on Qwen3.5-9B and 0.766 for responses on Qwen3-8B. On RTP-LX queries, PGuard-ema (Qwen3.5-9B) is the strongest native entry at 0.847, below Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B (0.877). On RTP-LX responses, PGuard-lasttok (Qwen3-8B) achieves the highest F1F_{1} of 0.898. For multimodal queries on Lingua-SafetyBench, PGuard-gru (Qwen3.5-9B) leads at 0.788, compared with 0.761 for HiddenDetect and 0.509 for Llama Guard 4.

4.3 Low Over-Refusal on Benign Traffic

Over-Refusal.

Table 7 reports over-refusal rates on XSTest and OR-Bench, measuring the cost of false blocks on benign content. PGuard-ema (Qwen3-8B) has an average query-side rate of 6.12%, within the range of the external baselines. Other PGuard variants reach 13.63–15.35%, below SIREN (22.41%) and NExT-Guard (17.38%). For responses, PGuard-ema (Qwen3.5-9B) achieves the lowest native average of 4.20%. Both sequence variants reduce response-side over-refusal relative to the stateless variant on each backbone.

Real-World Benign Traffic.

Tables 8 and 9 report interception rates on benign text and multimodal traffic. On text, PGuard variants intercept an average of 3.69–5.05% of queries and 2.32–2.80% of responses. Query-side rates are lower than those of both Qwen3Guard variants, whereas response-side rates are broadly comparable to external baselines. GRU and EMA show comparable interception rates across backbones. On multimodal traffic, average interception rates range from 0.11% to 0.60% for queries and from 0.07% to 0.18% for responses.

4.4 Early-Interception Analysis

The preceding evaluations measure sample-level classification, allowing comparison with detectors that assess completed responses. We next examine when PGuard first detects an unsafe response during generation.

For each detected unsafe response in the response-side benchmarks, we replay the sequence variant’s token-level risk trajectory. The interception point is the first position where the score crosses the threshold, expressed as a fraction of the full response length. We aggregate these fractions across benchmarks. A detector applied only after completion has an interception point of 1.01.0.

Figure 5(a) shows that 86.3% of detected unsafe responses are flagged within the first 10% of generated tokens, and 92.3% within the first 20%. These early flags allow generation to stop well before completion. With p=10p=10, the wait from any token to the next scoring point is at most nine decode steps. This brief scheduling delay is acceptable for monitoring risk that develops over phrases and passages, while avoiding unnecessary scoring at every token.

Prefix stability.

We evaluate prediction stability on S-Eval by measuring, among samples flagged by the guardrail, the proportion containing at least kk consecutive tokens with risk scores above 0.50.5, indicating sustained predictions of unsafe content. We consider k∈{5,10,20,50}k\in\{5,10,20,50\}. As shown in Figure 5(b), the ema-based variants maintain high stability as the required consecutive span increases: over 95% of threshold-hit samples sustain above-threshold scores for at least 20 tokens, and approximately 93% do so for 50 tokens. In contrast, the stateless variants show a more pronounced decline, with only 60–69% of samples sustaining the threshold for 50 tokens. The results suggest that temporal modeling produces more persistent risk predictions than relying solely on the last-token representation, particularly over longer spans.

4.5 Signal Analysis

Layer-gate profiles.

Figure 6 shows how learned layer-gate weights evolve during training. The weights concentrate on different layer subsets across backbones, supporting backbone-specific selection of capture layers.

Modeling variants on the spectrum.

Table 10 summarizes performance across backbones and representation-modeling variants. The stateless variant remains competitive on several tasks, including cyber and CBRN risk classification, whereas sequence modeling generally improves response detection. On Qwen3.5-9B, GRU and EMA-attention achieve text-response F1F_{1} scores of 0.860 and 0.833, respectively, compared with 0.795 for the stateless variant. For multimodal responses, the corresponding scores are 0.798, 0.772, and 0.644. GRU performs better on these response tasks, but requires a recurrent state update at every decode step. EMA-attention supports parallel prefill computation and remains the default sequence variant (Section 3.2). The choice therefore depends on the task and serving constraints.

4.6 Generalization Across Backbones

Table 10 covers Qwen backbones from 8B to 122B total parameters, including dense and MoE architectures and text-only and multimodal models. The same training recipe applies across these backbones, with layer selection and guard training performed separately for each backbone. These results highlight the applicability of the training recipe across model scales, with the benefits of larger backbones varying by task.

4.7 Serving Efficiency

Setup.

We measure the serving cost of PGuard with SGLang on L20Z GPUs. Appendix D lists the serving configuration of each backbone in Table 21. Each run uses a concurrency of 8 and 256 requests per scenario. The input length is 2048, 4096, or 8192 tokens, and the output length is 512 tokens. Each configuration is paired with a run of the bare backbone on the same node, and the two runs alternate in order across 4 rounds. We report the relative increase of time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT), together with the relative loss of output throughput. The bare backbone and PGuard use the same memory fraction for static allocation.

End-to-end overhead.

Table 11 reports TTFT, TPOT, and output throughput changes with each backbone’s best combination of optimizations across three backbones and input lengths of 2048–8192 tokens. Among the available measurements, the largest increases are 3.56% for TTFT and 3.07% for TPOT. For the stateless variant, the maxima are 1.54% and 1.78%, respectively; for EMA-attention, they are 3.56% and 2.40%. The GRU variant has maxima of 1.38% and 3.07%. Output throughput drops by at most 1.73% for the stateless variant and 2.26% for EMA-attention. Most entries stay below 2.5%, and all entries stay below 3.6%. This overhead is small and acceptable for large-scale production serving.

Ablation.

Tables 12 and 13 add the optimizations one at a time in the listed order. The full ladders reduce output throughput loss from 2.42–3.67% to 0.16–1.21% for the stateless variant and from 4.55–5.28% to 1.53–1.99% for EMA-attention. Selective decode scoring improves throughput across all three backbones, lowering throughput loss by 0.41–2.43 percentage points for the stateless variant and 0.92–2.19 percentage points for EMA-attention. The gains of the fusion and asynchronous copy steps depend on the backbone.

GRU end-to-end ablation.

Table 14 reports the end-to-end output throughput loss of the GRU variant relative to the bare backbone, with input/output lengths of 4096/512, concurrency 8, 256 requests, and four paired rounds. Lower values indicate less serving overhead. Async risk copy provides the largest reduction among adjacent reported configurations, bringing throughput loss to 1.16–1.75% across the three backbones. With selective decode scoring, the loss is further reduced to 0.90–1.09% across the three backbones.

Memory overhead.

PGuard maintains a small memory footprint alongside the backbone. Table 15 reports guard weights of 0.03–0.41 GiB per GPU, together with per-request state and peak workspace. Peak workspace remains below 0.5 GiB per GPU for the stateless variant and below 3.1 GiB per GPU for EMA-attention. The small memory overhead supports large-scale deployment of PGuard.

4.8 Deployment on the Cost–Accuracy Spectrum

Cost–accuracy overview.

Figure 7 summarizes the trade-off between detection accuracy and serving cost. GradSafe is omitted because it requires a backward pass to obtain gradients, which lies outside the serving forward path. Accuracy is measured on the benchmark suites above. Cost follows Section 3.2, with each configuration served by SGLang on the same GPU under saturation and normalized to the bare backbone. Serving a second large guard model raises normalized cost to as much as 2.7×\times. The plotted prior native guardrails achieve 0.64–0.74 macro F1F_{1} with 4–18% overhead. PGuard combines competitive accuracy with substantially lower serving overhead. On text, PGuard-gru reaches 0.848 macro F1F_{1}, exceeding Qwen3Guard-Gen’s 0.840, at 1.036×\times normalized cost. On multimodal inputs, PGuard-ema achieves 0.797 macro F1F_{1} at 1.019×\times cost, compared with 0.638 for the strongest prior native entry. These operating points pair strong detection quality with only 3.6% and 1.9% additional serving cost for text and multimodal inputs, respectively.

Two-tier deployment.

For deployments with a larger accuracy budget, the native variant composes with an external adjudicator instead of replacing it. Table 16 evaluates the two-tier deployment on S-Eval-Jailbreak, with Qwen3.5-Flash serving as both the PGuard backbone and the response generator. We regenerate the responses and cascade PGuard with an external reasoning-based guardrail. Jailbreak prompts are selected to increase the occurrence of risky responses, providing a stress test that approximates risky online traffic. It reaches the best overall score (96.72 average, versus 95.16 for PGuard alone), confirming that the native screen and the external adjudicator are complementary. Note that the gain comes entirely from precision, because recall is capped by the first tier. The adjudicator can only review traffic the native screen already flags, and this ceiling is intrinsic to any cascade. The economics of the pattern therefore hinge on the flagged fraction escalated to the second tier. On the Alpaca traffic set, the native guard flags 0.215% of responses, so only this fraction requires external review. This reduces second-tier calls by approximately 99.8% compared with reviewing every response. After review, the block rate falls to 0.056% (16 samples). The native guard therefore screens all traffic, while the external adjudicator reviews only flagged responses.

5 Background and Related Work

External guardrails.

External guardrails use a separate model to classify queries and responses. Llama Guard [Meta, 2025; Meta, 2024] uses instruction tuning with a content taxonomy, with its fourth generation supporting multimodal input. Related approaches include ShieldGemma [Google, 2024], Granite Guardian [IBM Research, 2024], NVIDIA’s Nemotron/Aegis safety models [NVIDIA, 2024], and ShieldLM [Zhang et al., 2024]. Qwen3Guard [Zhao and others, 2025] offers generative and streaming variants. The streaming variant adds classification heads to a base LLM to produce token-level verdicts. Despite its token-level outputs, Qwen3Guard-Stream still requires a separate LLM, adding model memory and inference computation beyond those of the protected backbone. SCM [Li et al., 2025b] likewise runs a separate Qwen2.5-7B model with token-level and sequence-level classification heads to monitor streamed responses, adding its own model memory and inference computation. WildGuard [Han et al., 2024] jointly classifies prompts, responses, and refusal behavior, while PolyGuard [Kumar and others, 2025] extends safety classification to 17 languages. GuardReasoner [Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b] and YuFeng-XGuard [Lin et al., 2026] generate explicit reasoning before a verdict, adding computation per request. For multimodal moderation, LlavaGuard [Helff and others, 2025] targets images, while SafeWatch [Chen et al., 2025] and OmniGuard [Zhu et al., 2025] extend coverage to video and omni-modal inputs. PolicyShiftGuard [Song et al., 2026] addresses cross-product policy adaptation, and JailGuard [Zhang et al., 2026] detects attacks through black-box input mutation. These approaches require serving an additional model. Response-level detectors also defer decisions until the response is complete.

Native guardrails: signal sources.

Native guardrails instead derive safety signals from the protected model. GradSafe [Xie and others, 2024] computes gradients for a paired compliant response and scores prompts using cosine similarity over safety-critical parameter slices. HiddenDetect [Jiang and others, 2025b] identifies unsafe multimodal inputs through refusal-related hidden-state directions before generation; Activation-Cone [Mitra, 2026] probes the first few generated tokens. SIREN [Jiao et al., 2026] trains lightweight per-layer probes over safety neurons, whereas kNNGuard [Abdelfattah et al., 2026] uses a nearest-neighbor bank of last-token activations. TrajGuard [Liu et al., 2026] monitors Mahalanobis distances along hidden-state trajectories, and Oldfield’s truncated polynomial classifier [Oldfield et al., 2026] examines higher-order residual-stream readouts. NExT-Guard [Fang et al., 2026a] selects safety-relevant sparse autoencoder features and scores them token by token. VLMGuard [Fang et al., 2026b] trains an MLP using SVD-derived pseudo-labels, while ARGUS [Lu et al., 2026] combines per-layer logistic probes with activation-level intervention for multimodal inputs. These approaches differ in their signal sources, decision granularity, and serving support, motivating joint evaluation of detection quality and runtime cost.

Native guardrails: streaming and production.

Streaming detection is the setting most closely related to PGuard. Segment-Level Coherence [He et al., 2026] pools windowed probe evidence for token-level decisions. Stop Early, Spend Less [Shu et al., 2026] integrates a probe into the vLLM decode loop for early termination. Kelp [Li et al., 2025a] models risk using a continuous-time latent state trained with response-level labels, while SafeSwitch [Han et al., 2025] combines a probe with a refusal head. Production systems also combine lightweight screening with more expensive adjudication. Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers combine an input classifier with an output value head [Sharma et al., 2025]. Its successor uses internal probes trained with sliding-window mean logit smoothing (SWiM) to flag traffic for a larger exchange classifier [Cunningham et al., 2026]. Google DeepMind’s Gemini probes [Kramár et al., 2026] similarly use token-level internal classifiers and escalate less than 10% of traffic. High-Stakes Probes [McKenzie et al., 2025] studies cascades that route a fixed fraction of traffic from a lightweight probe to an expensive judge. Together, these approaches motivate evaluating native screening as part of a complete serving pipeline.

Intervention mechanisms.

Other methods directly alter generation through representation reading and control [Zou et al., 2023], contrastive activation addition [Rimsky et al., 2024], or circuit breakers implemented with LoRA adapters [Zou et al., 2024]. Related approaches include learned null-space steering [Sheng et al., 2026] and multimodal defenses acting on prompts or activations [Wang et al., 2024; Gou et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025]. PGuard supplies token-level risk scores and leaves the response policy, such as reporting, interruption, or steering, to the deployment. These intervention mechanisms can therefore complement its detection interface.

Positioning of PGuard.

PGuard brings together representation-based safety detection and serving-engine integration, evaluating detection quality alongside runtime overhead. Its stateless and sequence variants offer different accuracy–cost trade-offs within a shared SGLang integration (Section 3). The evaluation spans dense and MoE backbones, text-only and multimodal models, and parameter scales from 8B to 122B (Section 4.6). The planned release includes the guard models, evaluation pipeline, and serving integration.

6 Conclusion

We presented PGuard, a native streaming guardrail that operates directly on the intermediate representations of a frozen backbone. Through dynamic layer gating, PGuard aggregates residual-stream features from selected layers, enabling a trained guard module to produce risk scores throughout both prefill and autoregressive decoding. We further explored three guard configurations: a stateless variant and two sequence-aware variants based on EMA-attention and GRU, offering different trade-offs between detection performance and serving efficiency.

Our evaluation across more than 30 benchmarks demonstrates that PGuard achieves competitive detection performance against dedicated external guardrails while consistently outperforming existing native baselines in aggregate. Its streaming predictions enable early detection of unsafe responses, allowing potential risks to be identified before generation is complete. Integrated into SGLang, PGuard incurs only 3.56% and 3.07% increases in TTFT and TPOT, respectively, across the evaluated serving configurations. These results demonstrate the practical viability of native guardrails for online safety screening, while retaining the option of external adjudication for flagged traffic. We are also extending the integration to vLLM, with adaptation work currently underway.

Limitations.

The effectiveness of PGuard depends on the extent to which safety-relevant information is encoded in the backbone’s intermediate representations. Attacks that induce harmful behavior without producing sufficiently informative signals in the captured representations may evade detection. Deep role-playing and fictional framing are potential examples that warrant targeted investigation. Furthermore, adapting PGuard to a new backbone requires calibration-set pretraining for layer selection, followed by guard-module training, even when the new backbone belongs to the same model family. These requirements introduce additional costs when deploying PGuard across different backbones.

Our current jailbreak evaluation relies on static benchmarks and does not establish robustness against adaptive attacks involving multi-turn interactions. Evaluating PGuard under dynamic red-teaming scenarios is therefore an important direction for future work. In addition, the framework leaves intervention policies to the deployment, motivating further investigation into how streaming risk scores can be translated into effective runtime actions. More expressive sequence models, including recurrent–EMA combinations and full self-attention, also merit exploration when serving budgets permit. Finally, we plan to extend the evaluation to larger backbones and additional modalities, and to release the guard models, benchmark pipeline, and SGLang serving integration alongside this work.
